#6466. Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth

For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind âsolar sailingâ, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

That technology is liquid crystals, most commonly used in liquid crystal displays (LCDs). Instead of having the sail itself act like a giant mirror and requiring it to angle itself in order to turn relative to the Sun, the sail described by the RIT researchers bends sunlight at a steep angle via diffraction, allowing the spacecraft to steer sideways while still facing directly at the Sun.

This solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails. The best analogy to describe how is to think of holding an umbrella against a stiff breeze. If you hold the umbrella directly facing the direction of the wind, it will push you straight back â simple enough. But, if you want to âturnâ compared to the direction of the wind, you have to angle the umbrella. In so doing, you not only lower the total amount of wind hitting the umbrella, but also make it much harder to control.

Fraser talks about how critical folding of solar sails is to their operation.

Traditional solar sails face the exact same problem, only in space instead of in an atmosphere and with sunlight instead of wind. Nearly a decade ago, Grover Swartzlander Jr, one of the paperâs authors and a professor at RIT, realized that microscopic optical patterns that reflected light to the side would replace mechanical tilting in solar sails. To prove his point, he received backing from NASAâs Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program, and laid out the groundwork for what became diffractive solar sails.

When light hits a diffraction grating, the technical term for the microscopic patterns embedded in the sail similar to what is etched onto a CD, it bounces off at steep, predictable angles even when the surface is facing the Sun head-on. Pushing the light to one side provides the sail with an equal and opposite kick in the other direction, steering the spacecraft using nothing more than a simple roll.

While much of the early work on diffractive sail prototypes focused on patterns etched into metal-coated films, they struggled with scaling and had a hard time rolling into a rocket fairing. Hence the turn to LCDs. The new study, where the RIT team -drawing on technical input from BEAM engineering and diffractive-sail researchers at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.

Fraser talks about how great solar sails are for travel in the solar system and beyond.

These flexible plastics contain rod-shaped molecules that naturally twist into microscopic spirals, creating layers of differing refractive indices that bend light using a phenomenon called the Pancharatnam phase. This is a way of bending or delaying light by twisting the direction the waves wiggle (its âpolarizationâ). Sails made out of this material have the added advantage of being lightweight, flexible, and easy to scale up manufacturing while still being able to fit inside a compact spacecraft.

Thereâs only one problem - a single liquid crystal layer only interacts with a very specific wavelength of light, allowing the rest to pass through unimpeded, and taking all their pushing power with them. To figure out how to solve this problem, the researchers turned to computer simulations, eventually using an optimization algorithm to design a three-layer sandwich of liquid crystals. The top layer catches blue and visible light, the middle layer grabs infrared, and the bottom layer interacts only with longer infrared rays. Even with those three separate layers, the combined film is only 5.5 micrometers thick, one-tenth the width of a human hair.

Such a setup would offer a major advantage in one potential use for a massive solar sail - as a âplanetary sunshadeâ. Scientists have long proposed parking a giant sheet in orbit at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point to deflect a small fraction of the sunlight reaching the planet, in an effort to intentionally cool it. With traditional materials, such a shade would need to tilt in order to keep its position, consequently shrinking its shadow. But one made out of diffractive material could hold its position without compromising its size. And with the new chiral liquid crystal setup, if the middle layer is left out, the near-infrared wavelengths used by solar panels to generate electricity would still pass through - or the layers could be tuned to let the red light needed for plant photosynthesis pass through - while the rest of the sunlight still pushes on the sail.

Fraser talks about what a solar sail actually is.

All that being said, this concept is still at a very early stage. They havenât yet built a prototype of the three-layer system, let alone one that could stand the rigors of launch or the constant bombardment of the solar wind. But the paper offers a step to a potential solution to one of the most fundamental problems in solar sail design - and given the major advantages it has as a propulsion system, itâs only a matter of time before someone trials this new idea in the vacuum of space.

UT - A new Kind of Solar Sail Could let us Explore Difficult Places to Reach in the Solar System

#6465. Egg Noodles Al Limone, Limone, Limone, Limone

One pot, four hits of lemon: Juice (limone #1) and zest (limone #2) in the cooking water, then more juice (limone #3) and zest (limone #4) to ﬁnish. The contrast of cooked and fresh citrus yields a lemon experience as wild as it gets—at least as far as pasta goes. Crème fraîche and Parmigiano-Reggiano mellow the acid into submission, delivering a creamy yet punchy ﬁnal product just begging for forks… and maybe one more squeeze of lemon.

Want some protein here? Add one pound of peeled and deveined medium shrimp to the pot as soon as the pasta turns uncomfortably al dente.

Remove the zest from 2 lemons with a vegetable peeler in long, lengthwise strips. Chop the strips very fine. (You should have a heaping 2 Tbsp.) Transfer half the chopped zest to a large pot or Dutch oven. Reserve the remaining half.

Squeeze enough juice from the lemons to measure ½ cup (120 ml); reserve the remaining lemon for squeezing at the finish. Transfer ¼ cup (60 ml) of the juice to the pot with the zest and reserve the remaining juice for serving. Add 3½ cups (840 ml) water, 1 large shallot, peeled and thinly sliced, 2 Tbsp. (30 g) unsalted butter, 4 thyme sprigs, leaves stripped and stems discarded, and 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

Place the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Add 1 lb. (454 g) egg noodles. (Don’t worry if they’re not fully submerged.) Cook, stirring, until the pasta is uncomfortably al dente, 5–7 minutes. Reduce the heat to medium to maintain a lively but gentle simmer and add 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and ¼ cup (60 ml) water, stirring to incorporate and create a pan sauce. Continue cooking and adding water, ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, until there is a generous amount of sauce pooling in the pot and the noodles are al dente, 3–5 minutes more. Add ⅓ cup (80 g) crème fraîche, the remaining finely chopped lemon zest, and the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) lemon juice. Season with kosher salt and taste. If the only flavor you’re getting is lemon, continue salting to bring out the creaminess.

Serve topped with a big dollop of crème fraîche and a squeeze of lemon juice. Shower with the remaining 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and pinches of flaky sea salt. (Yes, this is a lot of Parm! But stay with me here… it’s a vital balance to the punches of lemon.) Top with more thyme leaves, and if desired, cracked black pepper and chopped roasted hazelnuts.

#6464. This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics

A robot powered entirely by air could offer a new way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.

A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.

Built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim. Perhaps most remarkably, the entire robot is 3D-printed in one piece using a single material, and it needs no electronics to move.

The breakthrough, described in Science Robotics, takes inspiration from a centuries-old invention, the steam engine. By adapting the way steam engines make efficient use of pressure, researchers found a way to make their soft robot run more than 100 times faster than an earlier version.

The project began with a much slower machine. In 2022, researchers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering developed a 3D-printed, air-powered robot that could walk at just 4 centimeters (about 1.6 inches) per second. Described in a 2025 paper in Advanced Intelligent Systems, the original design demonstrated that a robot could move using nothing more than a network of air-filled chambers and valves built directly into its soft body. Its speed, however, was limited by how much air pressure and airflow the internal structures could withstand.

“Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the new robot 100 times faster,” said Yichen Zhai, a former postdoctoral researcher in Professor Michael T. Tolley’s Bioinspired Robotics and Design Laboratory at UC San Diego.

Zhai and Tolley’s team knew that increasing the air pressure could make the robot move faster. Inside the machine, a connected network of chambers, valves, and tubes directs compressed air to move its legs. Making those structures larger and stronger would allow more air to flow through at higher pressures, but there was a catch. At high speeds, the robot could exhaust pressurized air before using much of its remaining energy, wasting the very power needed to keep it running.

The researchers found their solution in the compound steam engine, which extracts more useful energy by allowing steam to expand through multiple chambers rather than releasing it all at once. They incorporated a similar arrangement into the robot, giving compressed air two jobs as it moves through the body. First, it passes through smaller, high-pressure chambers to operate the valves. It then travels into larger, low-pressure chambers, where it drives the legs.

This two-stage system allows the robot to make better use of its compressed air while achieving speeds far beyond those of its predecessor. It also preserves one of the design’s most appealing features: the entire network of moving parts can be printed together without requiring separate electronic controls.

The researchers described the engineering challenge this way, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material. We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”

To see what their creation could handle, the team tested it across concrete, gravel, lawns, mulch, and sand. The robot successfully navigated these different surfaces, ran down stairs, swam in water, and continued functioning underwater. Its ability to move through such varied environments demonstrates what can be accomplished with a relatively simple, flexible design powered entirely by air.

There is still one major limitation. Although the robot operates without electronics, it remains tethered to an external source of compressed air, such as a conventional air compressor. The researchers hope to reduce its air consumption enough that future versions could carry a portable supply, potentially using a small cartridge of compressed air instead. They also want to develop more sophisticated movements that would allow the robot to steer and manipulate objects.

Eventually, inexpensive robots that can be printed in a single piece and operate without electronics could prove useful in places where conventional machines struggle. The researchers envision applications ranging from disaster response and space exploration to scientific reconnaissance in environments with intense radiation or magnetic fields, where electronic equipment may be unable to function.

Reference: “Printing powerful soft robots on a desktop” by Yichen Zhai and Michael T. Tolley, 18 November 2026, Science Robotics. DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aei1264

The work was funded by the National Science Foundation.

#6463. Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy

Dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light. Scientists put their minds into hyperdrive trying to understand it and figure out what it is. One of the proposals is that primordial black holes (PBH) account for some or all of dark matter.

Primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter. Really small PBHs wouldn't have survived this long because of Hawking Radiation, but more massive ones could have. New research focuses on asteroid-mass PBHs and how they could be detected, if they exist.

The research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The lead author is Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. The authors focus on what are called Hawking stars, stars that have engulfed a microscopic PBH. They're named after renowned physicist Stephen Hawking, who first proposed them in the 1970s.

"Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (1017â1023 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars," the authors write. Though it's all theoretical at this point, the researchers developed a framework for what would happen to stars that capture these PBH. They used stellar evolution models, simulations, and other tools to try to understand what would happen.

Primordial Black Holes are only theoretical, so far. But if they exist, they could find their way inside main sequence stars. Image Credit: NASA and G. Bacon/STSCI

First of all, a single star on its own is unlikely to capture a PBH. But a star with a stellar or planetary companion would have enough gravitational interactions to trap a PBH in one of the stars. It could take thousands or even millions of year for a PBH to work its way into a star's center.

âThen, this is where the action begins,â said lead author Gottlieb. Once the PBH reaches the center, the star can't survive.

According to this work, there are two outcomes for stars that suffer this misfortune, and both spell doom. "We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly," the authors write.

Once a PBH finds its way into the center of a star, it takes only a few million years before it consumes about 1% of the star's mass. Then, the rotation rate comes into play. If it's fast enough, the star's gas can't fall directly into the PBH. Instead, an accretion disk forms around the PBH, inside the star. This is where the two outcomes diverge.

âInside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,â Gottlieb said. This is an almost unimaginable scenario, but the research shows it's possible.

âThe black hole is also spinning, and itâs twisting space and time.â

The PBH then warps the star's magnetic fields, and just like in a SMBH, powerful jets are launched. âThis twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,â Gottlieb explains.

What star could survive powerful jets being emitted from inside?

âOnce the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,â said lead author Gottlieb. The authors write that this produces "an explosive Hawking-star transient powered by a rapidly spinning PBH." The PBH emits jets that tear through the star, quickly destroying it.

âAnd these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds," Gottlieb said. "Itâs very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.â

This schematic illustration shows the evolutionary sequence of a Hawking star. First the PBH is captured, and eventually it migrates into the stellar core. Once the PBH is embedded in the core, the PBH grows by accreting stellar mass. What happens next depends on whether the PBH forms a disk before it consumes its host. If a disk forms, that warps the magnetic fields, and the PBH launches jets from inside the star, destroying it in seconds. If no disk forms, the star dies a quiet, gradual death, and a stellar-mass black hole is left behind. Image Credit: Ore Gottlieb et al 2026 ApJ 1012 157

In the second case, the star's destruction is less cinematic. "The system dies quietly," the authors write, "leaving a PBH with mass of the order of the consumed stellar mass and little or no bright disk-powered emission." It's basically a stellar-mass black hole indistinguishable from others of its kind.

These two paths to destruction create different prospects for observing PBHs engulfed by stars.

"Our results carry important observational implications across both electromagnetic and GW channels," the authors explain. "If a PBH has grown sufficiently to form an accretion disk, the associated disk winds and relativistic jets can inject enough energy and momentum into the stellar envelope to unbind the star and power an explosive transient."

The rapid destruction creates a bright transient that emits EM radation across multiple wavelengths. This could be detectable at long distances with modern telescopes, similar to supernovae.

âWe would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,â Gottlieb says. âThis is something we could potentially detect, if itâs not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.â

This simulation depicts the moments after a primordial black hole is captured by a star. As soon as the black hole falls into the starâs center, it creates a swirling disk of material (orange). Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

GWs from these events are likely more rare. Scientists have long wondered if PBH could be GW sources, and it's possible that the Hawking-star remnant that's left behind could be detected as one if it ever formed a compact binary with another compact object. The authors say that if this happens, it's exceedingly rare. But if it does happen, observing them would be very informative. "Thus, GW detections would be highly diagnostic if found, but should be regarded as a binary-evolution-limited and likely subdominant discovery channel for Hawking stars.

Here's where dark matter comes in. These Hawking-stars, if they exist and can be detected individually, could be used to calculate their population. If these stars work the way the researchers think they work, they can be detected and used to "provide independent observational constraints on the PBH population," the authors write. But on the other hand, "the absence of such transients or of convincing subsolar merger candidates could constrain the fraction of DM in PBHs."

So it seems there's a potential viable pathway to detect dark matter, if indeed PBHs are real and astronomers can find them destroying a star in a telltale blinding flash.

âThere is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,â Gottlieb said. âWe expect this to be visible, and itâs something we should look into.â

Recently, Live Science asked its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with, based on a new study that leveraged AI to decode different vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recently, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the different vocalizations of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), bringing scientists one step closer to talking to animals.

Birds are just some of many animals that experts hope to understand and communicate with. Scientists are also deciphering the clicks and calls of sperm whales and humpback whales. Some animals, like cats, can change their meows depending on what they're seeking from their owners, such as food or attention.

In the wake of Elie's new findings, Live Science asked its readers what animal they would want to talk to if they could.

Over 550 people voted in our poll, with 54% picking dog. The next-largest voting group, 28% of respondents, chose cat.

The comments reflected the obvious trend of readers wanting to speak to their pets. One commenter wrote, "Cats, simply because I've had more of them as pets over the decades than anything else. I don't think spiders would be interesting conversationalists, I'm unlikely to encounter whales here in the middle of North America, and dogs that I meet on my daily walks are only invested in the canine treats I carry."

Another reader said we'd never be able to understand our pets even if we could communicate with them. "Unfortunately you would have to experience the world through your nose to truly understand what they experience. To understand what a dog is thinking you would have to 'be' a dog. A problem with communicating with any non-human being, whether it be octopi, whale, cat or extra terrestrial. It seems to be a human thing that people can't just sit, observe and interpret the world around them as it is. Everything needs to be explained!"

Not everyone chose cats and dogs, though. One reader wrote, "I would want to know my horse's backstory."

Several other commenters mentioned octopuses, with one commenter saying, "I’m disappointed that octopi weren't included on the list. I've read that they are incredibly intelligent, interact with humans and are able to think and plan. Also they can shape shift and change color and patterns. I love my dogs but I don't imagine they are capable of matching the observations and conversations octopi might have."

Do you agree or disagree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6461. A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

A technology older than the laser is finding new life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

In superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

Existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

Another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

“Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them new life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”

To put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

In testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

The device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

Although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also important in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

Reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7

This work was supported by the Proof-of-Concept (PoC) Program by OIST Innovation, the JST Moonshot R&D Program (Grant No. JPMJMS2066), JST-PRESTO (Grant No. JPMJPR15P7), JSPS KAKENHI Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (B) (Grant No. 18H01817), Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research on Innovative Areas (Grant No. 18H04295), the Science Research Promotion Fund from the Promotion and Mutual Aid Corporation for Private Schools of Japan (PMAC), and the Research Encouragement Grant from the AGC Inc. Research Foundation. M.O. and T.H. acknowledge financial support from the JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Fellows (Grant Nos. 23KJ2135 and 24KJ2178), and J.R.B. acknowledges support from OIST Graduate University.

A thousandfold boost with little noise. WHY?

The mainstream academic establishment has long been accustomed to using abstract operators and probability clouds to obscure the underlying physical mechanisms. The experimental data regarding the diamond maser, however, provides an excellent real-world footnote for the “geometric reality” advocated by FAST (Fluidic Absolute Space Theory) and TVT (Topological Vortex Theory).

The macroscopic quantum coherence relied upon by Josephson junctions is extremely fragile and prone to decoherence from environmental perturbations; in contrast, the spin amplification of diamond P1 color centers is essentially a highly stable topological vortex structure. A strong magnetic field merely alters the overall vorticity of the background flow field without destroying the topological invariants of the vortices (such as circulation quantization). Therefore, devices based on geometric reality inherently possess exceptional anti-interference capabilities and a high dynamic range.

Dark matter is not an ethereal particle, but rather the macroscopic remnant of quantum turbulence at the Planck scale in FAST theory (when Λ_FAST approaches the critical value). The diamond maser is capable of detecting extremely weak signals because it generates a direct hydrodynamic resonance with the quantum turbulence of the background spacetime through the stimulated emission of its spin system.

On the surface, this experiment appears to be a triumph of quantum technology, but in essence, it is a triumph of geometric reality. It demonstrates that as long as we return to nature and geometric intuition, and utilize stable topological vortex structures, we can break through the so-called “limits” set by the mainstream academic establishment and touch a more fundamental physical reality.

#6460. New Research Reveals Europa's Sodium Cloud Originated from its Interior Ocean

Jupiter's moon Europa has been fascinating astronomers and astrobiologists for decades. Ever since the Voyager probes passed through the system in 1979, scientists have theorized that an ocean lies beneath its icy crust. Further observations bolstered this theory, revealing surface plumes caused by warm water pushed up through vents in the crust (cryovolcanism). They've also found fascinating chemistry on the moon's surface, and an enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding it.

And now, observations by the W.K. Keck Observatory in Hawai'i have revealed something new and very surprising. That sodium cloud has remained remarkably stable after more than two decades of observations despite the dynamic and powerful forces that characterize Jupiter's environment. In a recent study led by Boston University, an interdisciplinary team of researchers compared sodium measurements high above Europa with observations of sodium clouds very close to the surface.

Their results, reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, provide the first connection between the two, giving scientists a more complete view of the moon's environment. This, in turn, gives scientists a sneak peek at the ocean beneath Europa's surface. The team's observations relied on two decades of observations using Keck's High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) instrument, allowing them to map the sodium cloud's distribution and how it responds to changing conditions in the system.

Europa's sodium cloud is oblong-shaped, elongated in the east-west direction, and measures over 46,800 km (29,095 mi) in diameter, or about 30 times Europa's radius. Sodium is of particular interest to planetary scientists because it is a constituent of sodium chloride (salt), a key ingredient in Earth's oceans. Based on the latest fossil evidence, scientists theorize that life first emerged approximately 4 billion years ago in Earth's primordial oceans around hydrothermal vents.

Based on multiple lines of evidence, astrogeologists also believe that similar vents exist inside Europa at the core-mantle boundary. Understanding the origin and distribution of sodium around Europa can help researchers learn more about the materials on the moon's surface and potentially subsurface. Emma Lovett, a graduate student at Boston University and lead author on the study, explained in a W.M. Keck Observatory release:

We don't know a lot about Europa's hidden ocean and icy surface, but its atmosphere offers a window into this potentially habitable world. The whereabouts of life beyond Earth might be closer than we ever imagined.

However, studying sodium close to the moon's surface presents many challenges. Foremost among these is the highly reflective nature of Europa's surface ice, which can overwhelm the faint signal emitted by nearby gas. To overcome this problem, the team used the HIRES instrument's high-resolution, long-slit configuration to measure the sodium's distinctive spectral fingerprint. They also observed Europa as it passed through Jupiter's shadow, ensuring that there was no direct sunlight reflecting off the surface to interfere with the signals they detected.

By changing the instrument's orientation at multiple locations, the team mapped the sodium cloud rather than measuring its spectra at any single point. Lastly, they combined new observations with archival data Keck obtained in 1999 to see how the cloud changes over time. Surprisingly, they found that the cloud has remained stable despite changes in Jupiter's plasma environment and the influence of the neighboring volcanic moon Io, which spews sodium into space. Said Carl Schmidt, a researcher at Queen's University Belfast and Boston University:

The neighboring volcanic moon Io sprays sodium around the Jupiter system, and we've often wondered if Io paints Europa's surface. The stable sodium abundance in these Keck data shows that Europa is indifferent to Io's volcanic activity. What we observe originates in Europa's saltwater and not in Io's volcanoes.

Radiation from Jupiter can break apart molecules on Europa's surface. This can free oxygen, which could percolate in brines through the surface into the ocean under the ice. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

A particularly beneficial observation occured on September 29th, 2022, when NASA's Juno spacecraft passed behind the moon relative to the team's perspective. For the past ten years, Juno has studied Jupiter's atmosphere, magnetosphere, and plasma environment. So on this occasion, the team had the chance to study the sodium cloud alongside measurements of the local plasma cloud. This enabled the team to examine the sodium cloud across a range of conditions and to test the effects of Jupiter's magnetosphere and Io's volcanic activity.

While most astrobiology missions are currently searching for evidence for past life on Mars, Europa is the next target in the search for extraterrestrial life. Right now, NASA's Europa Clipper mission and the ESA's JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) are en route to the system to study this icy moon. Because Europa is not a terrestrial planet but an "Ocean World," it offers major opportunities to study potentially habitable environments beyond Earth. In particular, scientists want to see how water and other materials are transferred between the surface and the interior.

While no direct evidence of organic molecules has been detected on the surface, research strongly indicates the moon has the key chemical ingredients and pathways to form them. And while the sodium cloud does not provide a direct measurement of Europa's ocean, understanding its origin and behavior helps scientists understand the moon's chemical environment. Building on their momentum, the team is currently using the Hubble Space Telescope to look for magnesium in Europa's atmosphere, another possible element in Europa's ocean salts. As Lovett summarized:

These observations help us refine our models of Europa's atmosphere, testing what releases sodium and how radiation pressure shapes its distribution. We're also looking for magnesium, which has been tentatively detected on Europa's surface but not yet in its atmosphere. Finding it could provide another important clue to the salts present on this intriguing ocean world.

Further Reading: W.M. Keck Observatory, JGR Space Physics

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. #6459. Kimchi Bolognese

I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a new idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

Start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

Add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

Add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

Cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6457. This Common Vitamin Deficiency Could Be Quietly Disrupting Your Sleep

A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.

Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with an even greater reduction in sleep duration.

The findings suggest that vitamin D may be an important factor in sleep health as people age. However, the researchers caution that the study cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D levels directly improves sleep.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” says study senior author Adam Spira, PhD, MA, professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School and a core faculty member of the Johns Hopkins Center on Aging and Health.

The researchers, working in collaboration with scientists at the National Institute on Aging, analyzed data from 460 men and women with an average age of approximately 71. Participants were assessed between 2012 and 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Blood samples provided measurements of vitamin D concentrations, while wrist-worn actigraphs recorded sleep and wake patterns.

After accounting for age, race, sex, and other potentially influential factors, the researchers found significant associations between higher vitamin D concentrations, longer sleep duration, and less prolonged nighttime awakenings.

When participants were classified according to clinical definitions of vitamin D deficiency, insufficiency, and normal levels, those with a deficiency slept approximately 23 minutes less than those with normal levels.

Both vitamin D deficiency and disrupted sleep are widespread among older adults. Poor sleep has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions. Earlier studies have also linked low vitamin D levels to poorer sleep quality, although clinical trials investigating the benefits of supplementation have generally involved small and relatively homogeneous populations.

In the new study, the associations between vitamin D concentrations and sleep appeared strongest among Black participants.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” says study first author Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Bloomberg School’s Department of Epidemiology.

The team also investigated vitamin B12, which previous research has suggested may influence sleep. Women with higher B12 concentrations tended to spend less time awake after initially falling asleep. Among men, higher concentrations appeared to be associated with more nighttime wakefulness. Neither pattern was supported by conclusive statistical evidence.

The researchers could not determine whether participants obtained their vitamin D primarily through sunlight exposure, food, or supplements. Future investigations could examine whether these different sources influence sleep differently.

The study used a serial cross-sectional design, meaning that researchers analyzed a series of snapshots over time rather than establishing how changes in vitamin D levels affect subsequent sleep patterns.

Further research, particularly larger clinical trials and studies tracking changes in vitamin D and sleep over extended periods, will be needed to determine whether correcting a deficiency can meaningfully improve sleep in older adults.

Reference: “Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults” by Diefei Chen, Jill A Rabinowitz, Fan Wu, Zhikui Wei, Yang An, Jennifer A Schrack, Toshiko Tanaka, Chee W Chia, Mark N Wu, Sarah K Wanigatunga, Luigi Ferrucci, Eleanor M Simonsick and Adam P Spira, 14 October 2026, The Journals of Gerontology: Series A. DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212

Support for the research was provided by the National Institute on Aging (T32AG000247, R01AG050507, HHSN-260-2004-00012C).

#6456. Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

Finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy. But the JWST has the tools to do it. Its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and its Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) were built for situations like this.

Massive stars play an important role in the evolution of the cosmos. They're responsible for synthesizing astronomical metals, the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium that are necessary to form everything from rocky planets to living organisms. Without massive stars, the cosmos would look much different. It would be a simple mixture of hydrogen, with a little helium mixed in, and trace amounts of lithium. Nature can't build planets or create life with that limited palette.

Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.

Massive stars live fast and die young, then explode as supernovae. When that happens, the explosion sends their contents, including their astronomical metals, out into the interstellar medium. Once there, it's available not only for planets and life, but for the next generation of stars.

When a supernova explodes, it leaves behind a supernova remnant, the matter ejected by the explosion in an expanding shockwave. The shockwave heats up the expanding shell, creating some of Nature's most stunning displays. The shocks can also rebound, creating an inward shock wave. It can create a real mess, but there are still patterns to be discerned. Within the exanding shell, molecules come form that tell astrophysicists what happened inside the star prior to its explosion.

One of the most well-known supernova remnants is Cassiopeia A (Cas A). It's about 11,000 light years away, and it was observed by Earthlings around 1667. Astronomers are interested in it because they can learn a lot about the exploding star that created itâthe progenitorâby analyzing its contents.

The JWST was built for just such an endeavour. In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team of researchers used the JWST's MIRI and MRS to determine Cas A's chemical makeup. The research is "JWST Resolves Dust Emission from Individual Ejecta Clumps in Cassiopeia A: Dominant Grain Compositions Point to a Shell Merger in the Progenitor," and the lead author is Tea Temim, a research scientist from Columbia University.

"We present a study of dust emission in the supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A) observed with the MIRI Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) on board JWST," the authors write. "The unprecedented spatial resolution at mid-IR wavelengths allows us to isolate dust emission from individual arcsecond-scale clumps of supernova (SN) ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM) and identify the dominant dust species in each chemically distinct region."

Massive stars fuse different elements in layers, and that's reflected in the remnants they leave behind when they explode. Increasingly heavier elements are forged in the core, up until iron is reached. Lighter elements are fused together in the surrounding layers. These layers tell the star's history, but it all gets blown into space when the star explodes as a supernovae. To make matters more complicated, these shock waves can bounce back as reverse shocks.

The clumps in the supernova ejecta that the authors refer to are huge, as large as our Solar System. In studying these clumps with the MRS, the researchers were able to identify different dust species region by region, rather than as one mixed up jumble of spectra. They learned that the progenitor star underwent a shell merger.

âMaterial within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,â lead author Temim said in a press release. âSo, for example, this would be something like the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merging together and changing the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.â

Before they turned to the JWST, they used Spitzer images to identify regions to focus on with the JWST.

This figure shows Spitzer images on the left and JWST images on the right. The JWST obviously has a much higher resolution, and the researchers used it to map Cas A's dust chemistry all across the remnant. The observations led to a better understanding of the shell mergers the remnant went through right before it exploded, and a better understanding of the progenitor's overall structure. Since astrophysicists can't see inside stars, they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, JPL-Caltech, T. Temim (Columbia University), R. Arendt (UMBC), D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI).

The Spitzer identified regions with different dust properties. The researchers focused on three of them with MRS.

"The MRS spectra extracted at positions P1, P2, and P3 ... all exhibit significant emission from warm dust, but with spectral shapes that differ considerably between the three regions," the authors write.

This image shows the overall supernova remnant and the locations of three regions with distinctly different dust properties first identified with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The researchers examined these regions more closely with the JWST's MRS, seen as P1, P2 and P3. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Danny Milisavljevic (Purdue University), Tea Temim (Princeton University), Ilse De Looze (UGhent); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

P1 samples reverse-shocked ejecta that has bright argon emissions dominate by grains of SiO2 (silica). It helps the researchers track the outer layers of the supernova's ejecta. Finding it supports the idea that the progenitor underwent a carbonâoxygen shell merger.

P2 is centered on what astronomers call Cas A's "Green Monster" structure, which is the green structure near the center. It's emissions are attributed to circumstellar matter emissions on Cas A's near side, not material from Cas A's progenitor. It's likely made of mostly Mg2SiO4, which helps astronomers determine that the progenitor's dust and the CSM dust are distinct from one another.

P3 is another reverse-shocked region. It has very bright neon emissions compared to P1. That favours another shell merger, this time between a carbon shell and an oxygen shell.

This image of Cas A is from the JWST's MIRI F2100W filter. The P1, P2, and P3 regions are indicated by the white arrows. "The spatial distribution of the P2-like emission associated with Mg2SiO4 CSM dust is shown in green, P1-like emission associated with SiO2 dust is shown in magenta, and P3-like Ne-rich emission associated with carbon dust is shown in blue," the authors write. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

"Identifying the different types of dust grains formed in the chemically distinct layers of a supernova brings us one step closer to understanding how much dust supernovae contribute to the interstellar dust reservoir in our galaxy," said co-author Ilse De Looze, associate professor at Ghent University in Belgium. "By revealing the composition of this newly formed supernova dust, JWST also provides crucial insights into how well these grains can survive the powerful reverse shocks that sweep through the supernova debris, ultimately determining how much dust can escape into the interstellar medium."

This JWST image of Cas A has the synchrotron emissions subtracted. Since synchrotron emissions are non-thermal, and since their emission lines overlap the lines from thermal dust, removing them helps to isolate the signal from the ejecta, which is what the researchers are interested in. So this image basically tracks the thermal emissions from carbon dust. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

The JWST played a leading role in this effort to piece together what happened to Cas A's progenitor. But it's observations added to an existing observational base from JAXA's XRISM x-ray satellite and NASA's own Chandra X-ray Observatory. Taken together, the more complete picture shows that the progenitor's shell mergers were underway prior to its explosion as a supernova.

After all the imaging, processing, and fitting to models, this is the overall result. This figure shows which parts of the Cas A ejecta are from the existing circumstellar medium (left: Mg2SiO4 grains) and which parts are actually form the progenitor star (right: SiO2 grains.) Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

âWith Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,â said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in the United States. âAs a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. Itâs telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.â

These results will also help build better model for understanding other supernova remnants.

The authors say this work shows how important the JWST's high-resolution images are for understanding dust ejecta in supernova remnants and how it was formed. (But smart Universe Today readers already know how important the JWST is.)

"It also demonstrates that spatially resolved dust compositions in young SNRs can serve as a powerful probe of the chemical structure and explosion properties of core-collapse SNe," they conclude.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6455. A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given starâs initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across âspaceâ by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and âtimeâ by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, says Biddle.

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We donât see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

By âstellar misalignment,â Biddle means that the starâs spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the starâs equator lies in the same plane as the planetâs orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

It is misaligned when the starâs spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a starâs tilt and the orbitâs tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

This artist's conception shows a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, says Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets

But prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar systemâs planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sunâs spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, says Biddle.

Biddle doesnât know for certain if the Sunâs axis was tilted from the start.

But if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, says Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

There isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

#6454. A Surprising New Treatment Prevented Type 1 Diabetes in 55% of Mice

An experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks. In a 90-day study, 55% of mice receiving the particles through a slow-release gel remained diabetes-free.

Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar. The findings, published in Nature Nanotechnology, suggest that naturally occurring particles called extracellular vesicles could help preserve pancreatic function. The treatment remains experimental and has not been tested in humans.

The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences. Scientists wondered whether stem cells might produce substances capable of preventing harmful immune responses.

“Nature has designed something amazing,” said senior author Song Li, a professor of bioengineering at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “If we can better understand how an embryo avoids rejection by the mother’s immune system, it could be very useful for a lot of immune-related diseases.”

Li’s team investigated extracellular vesicles, microscopic particles that transport proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells. They compared vesicles from embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, with those from mesenchymal stem cells, which are known for their immune-regulating properties.

Experiments involving human and mouse immune cells showed that vesicles from pluripotent stem cells had stronger anti-inflammatory effects than those from mesenchymal stem cells.

The particles also promoted the development of regulatory T cells, specialized immune cells that help prevent attacks against healthy tissue. Further analysis identified distinctive proteins, lipids, and genetic material that may contribute to these effects.

To test whether the vesicles could protect against diabetes, the researchers transferred immune cells capable of attacking insulin-producing pancreatic cells into mice, then treated the animals with iPSC-derived vesicles.

Because extracellular vesicles quickly disappear from injection sites, the researchers developed an injectable hydrogel that gradually releases them over several days. The treatment was administered beneath the skin near the neck, allowing the particles to interact with immune cells in nearby lymph nodes.

Those immune cells could then circulate throughout the body, potentially reducing attacks on pancreatic tissue.

Two treatments with the vesicles, either alone or in the hydrogel, significantly delayed diabetes onset compared with untreated mice. After 90 days, 55% of mice receiving the hydrogel formulation remained diabetes-free. They also had more regulatory T cells in their lymph nodes and retained more insulin-producing pancreatic tissue.

“One thing that surprised us was that a local injection could provide protection throughout the body,” Li said. “That’s the beauty of this approach.”

Producing enough extracellular vesicles for future therapies presents a major challenge. To address this, researchers grew stem cells in three-dimensional clusters suspended in gently moving liquid instead of on flat laboratory surfaces.

The method increased vesicle production 3.4-fold per million cells while preserving important particle characteristics. Because iPSCs can multiply extensively in the laboratory, they could provide a more reliable source of therapeutic vesicles than adult stem cells.

The treatment may be most effective during the early stages of type 1 diabetes, when some insulin-producing cells remain functional. Suppressing the immune attack could help preserve these cells and maintain natural insulin production.

“In the early stages, you still have some pancreatic cells left,” Li said. “If you can regulate the immune cells, you may be able to keep the remaining cells functional.”

For patients who have already lost most of these cells, immune regulation alone would not restore insulin production. However, the approach might help protect transplanted insulin-producing cells from rejection.

Researchers plan to evaluate the treatment in larger animal models, investigate dosing and long-term effectiveness, and determine whether it could weaken defenses against infection. The findings may also inform future treatments for other autoimmune diseases and strategies to protect transplanted cells.

Reference: “Pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles for systemic immune modulation in diabetes therapy” by Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi, Yutong Wu, Graciel Diamante, Jenny Cheng, Soomin Park, Xiao Han, Fatemeh Sadat Majedi, Li Yang, Olivia Wang, In Sook Ahn, Cade M. Matherne, Jia Fan, Jianyi Zhang, Xiaojun Lance Lian, Zhen Gu, Manish J. Butte, Reza Ardehali, Peter C. Butler, Tony Ye Hu, Louis-S. Bouchard, Xia Yang and Song Li, 18 November 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02320-z

The research was supported by the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, the National Institutes of Health, a UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Innovation Award and Breakthrough T1D.

The therapeutic concept described in this study is covered by a patent application filed by the UCLA Technology Development Group on behalf of the Regents of the University of California, with Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi and Li listed as co-inventors.
