The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

#6425. A New Discovery is Re-Drawing the Map of the Milky Way

Star formation is a galaxy's foundational process. Astronomers study how star-forming gas moves around in a galaxy, where it's compressed, and in which parts of a galaxy stars form. In a barred spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, star formation is mostly concentrated in the spiral arms. In the central bar, star formation is more sluggish.

Recent research shows that though the central bar contains many stars, star formation there is mostly concentrated in the bar ends. Shear forces, streaming motions, and overpowering shocks that make the gas in the bars turbulent all combine to to inhibit star formation.

The Milky Way is a typical barred spiral galaxy, and astronomers have studied it intently to understand where star formation is concentrated. There's ongoing scientific debate about what happens in a barred spiral galaxy's central bar. Observations of other spiral barred galaxies show that star formation suppression there isn't necessarily universal. Part of the difficulty in understanding our own galaxy is observing the region. Since we're embedded in the galaxy, it's difficult to observe the bar. In many ways, astronomers have an easier time observing other galaxies.

Researchers from Australia and Sweden have found an unusual structure in the Milky Way's center that appears to set it apart from many other barred spiral galaxies. It's a vast collection of rotating stars in the central bar that's generating powerful and large shock fronts in the gas. These shock fronts are triggering star formation in the structure, which goes against the idea that stars can't form there.

The results are in new research titled "The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The lead author is Dr. Hilary Davis from the University of Sydneyâs School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy. The research is casting doubt on the existence of one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, the Norma arm.

This illustration shows the Milky Way's major and minor spiral arms, as well as its central bar. The Norma arm is close to the galaxy's center. Image Credit: NASA.

"The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Normaâouter arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated," the authors write. In past work, researchers have used astrophysical masers, which are coherent microwave emissions from young massive stars, to trace part of the Norma arm that extends from the central bar. So those results suggest that the masers reside along the Norma spiral arm.

But the Milky Way's bar is tricky to study. âThe Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view,â Dr Davis said. âAs a result, the barâs properties have been highly debated.â

This new research, based on observations and massive astrophysical simulations suggests that what those masers really trace is the shock front or dust lane in its bar. Since stars form along shock fronts where gas is compressed, star formation is at the heart of this work. "This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way," the authors explain.

This graphic shows modelling of the Milky Way with the Norma arm overlapping the bar shock front in the Milky Way. It's based on observations of masers from young stars. Previous research suggested those masers and young stars were in the Norma arm, but this work shows they're tracing star formation along a shock front in the Milky Way's central bar. Image Credit: Hillary Davis/University of Sydney

âAt its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale,â lead author Davis said.

Modern telescopes give us clear views of other galaxies on a regular basis. Observations of other spiral galaxies show that star formation is abundant in their spiral arms, where gas is compressed by density waves.

âIn most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. Whatâs extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed,â said Davis.

The researchers used large-scale astrophysical models run on powerful computers to try to understand the masers and what they meant for star formation, and what part of the Milky Way's structure they traced. They found that the masers indicated star formation along a shock front in the bar, not in the Norma arm. Observational challenges made it seem like those masers were in the Norma arm.

âWe believe that the Milky Wayâs bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies,â Dr Davis said.

This figure from the research shows how what appears to be a spiral arm with star formation is actually the shock front from the central bar where stars are forming. "The red scatter points with black borders are the Norma masers," the authors write, but they actually line up with the shock front and may not be a spiral bar at all. Image Credit: Davis, H., Bland-Hawthorn, J., Tepper-GarcÃ­a, T. et al. The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front. Nat Astron (2026).

"The Norma masers trace very young (âª1âMyr) star-forming regions that are still close to the gas clouds in which they formed because they have not had sufficient time to migrate away. Hence, the association of Norma masers with the Galactic bar shock front suggests that SF is occurring along the Galactic bar dust lane," the authors explain.

The result is that part of the Norma arm may have lost its status as a spiral arm.

âWe found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations,â Dr Davis said. âThis suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar."

These results show that stars can more readily form in the central bar, something that seemed prohibitive. âThis raises questions about the Galaxyâs spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation,â she said.

Astronomers have studied the Milky Way's central bar and argued about its nature for decades. There's been plenty of uncertainty about its properties and its role in star formation, and these results are shaping our understanding of the bar. âOur findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar,â Dr Davis said.

"By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a â 4.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, b â 2.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, Ï = 20(+5/-2)âand Î©p â² 40 km sâ1 kpcâ1, representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively," the authors write.

In plain language, they're saying that the bar's full, end-to-end length is about 28,000 light years, its width is about 15,000 light years, and it's tilted about 20 degrees from our line of sight. It also takes about 154 million years to complete one rotation.

For comparison, prior estimates of the bar's length range from 3,000 to 16,000 light years, and its width has been estimated between 8,000 and 16,000 light years. Measurements of its time to complete one rotation range from 102 to 246 million years. So these results are inside existing ranges.

The wide ranges for its size and rotation speed illustrate how difficult studying the bar is. The wide ranges may seem absurd, but astronomers have had limited observations to work with. Overall, these results add new constraints on the bar's properties, and they carry more weight based on how the researchers arrived at them.

âBy comparing a new generation of large-scale computerised galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way,â Dr Davis said.

The main finding is that the bar has the ability to form stars, and that may mean the Milky Way is different from many other barred spirals.

"This raises questions about the Milky Wayâs spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming," the authors write.

#6424. Scientists Simulated What May Happen If a Nuclear Bomb Goes Off in Space. The Fallout Is Terrifying.

Radioactive waste and resulting collisions would inflict the most damage as 98% of our satellites—and the tech that relies on them—would be wiped out.

If hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

When a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

“Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”

This is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or launched soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

The researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

Starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers said. “New satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”

#6423. Scientists Discover That Jupiter and Dead Stars Could Hold Clues to Dark Matter’s Biggest Mystery

The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering new clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen. Known as dark matter, it is thought to make up about 85% of all matter, yet its true nature remains a mystery. Researchers know it exists largely because of its gravitational effects, but they still do not know what it is made of.

Scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any. One possibility is that some particles move so slowly that they barely register in laboratory experiments. However, those same particles might be easier to find in places much larger than any detector on Earth: planets and stars.

Researchers Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard, and Gaurav Tomar investigated whether these celestial bodies could act as natural traps for dark matter. Their study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), found no evidence of dark matter but helped rule out certain possibilities about its properties.

Dark matter is known to interact through gravity, but scientists suspect it may also have extremely weak electrical or magnetic properties. Some particles could carry a tiny electric charge or behave like miniature magnets, allowing them to interact with ordinary matter in ways that are difficult to detect.

Speed could make those interactions even harder to observe. When a slow-moving particle strikes material inside a detector, it may transfer too little energy to produce a measurable signal. Inside a planet or star, however, even a small loss of energy could be enough to prevent the particle from escaping the object’s gravitational pull.

Over billions of years, these trapped particles could accumulate near the center of a planet or star. If their properties allow it, they might eventually collide and undergo a process called annihilation, transforming into other particles. Some of the resulting particles could escape into space, while others could release energy that warms the surrounding material.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” explains Gaurav Tomar, a researcher at the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea and the study’s corresponding author. “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”

The researchers used two different approaches to look for signs of dark matter. For Earth and the Sun, they examined existing searches for neutrinos, tiny particles that can travel through enormous amounts of matter without being stopped. If dark matter particles were annihilating deep inside these bodies, some of the resulting neutrinos might reach detectors and provide evidence of what was happening.

For Jupiter and white dwarfs, which are dense remnants of stars, the team looked at heat instead. Unlike the Sun, these objects are not powered by ongoing nuclear fusion, making them potentially useful places to investigate whether another source of energy is contributing to their warmth.

The researchers calculated how much heat different types of dark matter could produce if captured inside these objects, then compared those predictions with the energy the objects actually emit. If a particular type of dark matter would generate more heat than an object releases, that scenario could be ruled out.

By combining these calculations with existing observations, the team excluded several combinations of dark matter particle mass and electromagnetic properties that previous experiments had not eliminated. Earth was particularly useful for investigating particles with extremely small electric charges, while white dwarfs helped constrain other possible electromagnetic interactions.

The findings also come with an important uncertainty. How much dark matter a celestial body could capture depends partly on how much dark matter surrounds it. For white dwarfs in particular, researchers must rely on estimates because the local dark matter density is not always known.

“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar notes.

He was referring to the M4 star cluster, where the white dwarfs examined in the study are located. The amount of dark matter in that region has not been directly measured and must instead be estimated using models.

Looking ahead, Tomar suggests searching for even colder white dwarfs in regions thought to contain more dark matter. Because these stars emit relatively little heat, any additional warming from trapped particles could be easier to identify. Planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system could also offer new opportunities to investigate whether dark matter is quietly accumulating inside celestial bodies.

Reference: “Celestial probes of dark matter electromagnetic interactions” by Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard and Gaurav Tomar, August 27, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2608.27957

#6422. Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors

Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Societyâs Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.

Currently, space-based nuclear power is advancing under a NASA program known as the Space Power and Reactor Capabilities (SPARC) program. One crucial constraint in this plan to build a 40-kilowatt nuclear reactor on the Moon is its weight limit. Any system has to be under 6,000 kg in order to fit on a mobile rover on the lunar surface.

Thatâs not a lot of weight to work with for a nuclear reactor, especially one of that size. And in addition to being one of the most important health and safety parts of a reactor, shielding is also one of the heaviest. To lower the weight of their systems, space reactor designers have historically relied on directional âshadow shields.â Instead of encompassing an entire reactor with an absorbent material like lead or concrete, they use lightweight hydrogen-rich materials like lithium hydride combined with dense metal positioned in a specific direction to protect highly sensitive parts of the reactor itself, such as the control electronics.

Fraser talks in detail about the Kilopower reactor.

Directional shields mean the rest of the area around the reactor is left unprotected, which isnât great if part of that area is zoned for human habitation. Even 1 km away from the reactor site, the amount of radiation if left unprotected would be deadly. But bringing up even more shielding from Earth to protect any such habitation zone is extraordinarily expensive.

To solve this problem, the research team, led by Los Alamos researcher Alex Levinsky, turned to a simple solution â use natural lunar terrainâlike a crater depression or a dirt hillâto block the direct line of sight, and thereby most of the radiation from reaching the habitation area. Since building a mockup lunar nuclear reactor and procuring hundreds of tons of lunar regolith presumably wasnât in the budget for this research, the team turned to computer simulations instead.

They used a software called Monte Carlo N-Particle to simulate millions of subatomic particles emanating from the nuclear reactor core. Placing it 1.5 m off the ground allowed them to simulate its positioning on the back of a wheeled rover. They then started modeling what different kinds of barricades would look like between the reactor and the habitation space.

Fraser talks about lunar base site selection and why it needs a fission reactor.

First, their simulations focused on arbitrary landscapes, such as a three-meter-deep crater or a gently sloping three-meter-high dirt hill. Both effectively blocked almost all of the radiation coming from the reactor, knocking it down to roughly one-tenth of a rem per yearâabout fifty times lower than the five-rem-per-year limit set for reactor radiation above the Moon's natural background.

With that success in mind, the next task was to model an actual environment. The research team chose Connecting Ridge, a mountain ridge near Shackleton Crater at the Lunar South Pole. This is an ideal site for future crewed missions, as it combines two of the most sought-after features of the lunar landscape. Some of the ridges are in almost permanent sunlight, being lit 80-90% of the time, while also being right next to Permanently Shadowed Regions that never see the Sun at all and are home to deposits of water ice that is crucial to life support and rocketry in any future permanent colony.

When placing the reactor in this environment, the research team made sure to respect the limitations of the rover (no slopes more than 18 degrees), but managed to find a natural depression that could be separated from a simulated base camp by a 120-m-high crater wall. With that barrier in place, the radiation hitting the habitat from the reactor dropped to near zeroâonly about four-hundredths of a rem per yearâallowing the reactor's onboard shadow shield to focus solely on protecting nearby electronics.

Fraser talks about finding water ice in the Moon's Permanently Shadowed Craters.

One nice feature about the airless Moon in this context is the engineers donât have to deal with âskyshineâ â a phenomenon where radiation shot into the sky bounces off air particles there and bounces back down onto the habitat. Since the Moon has no atmosphere, there is nothing for the radiation to bounce off of, solving one of the problems with reactors on Earth.

However, there is one major catch. While placing regolith between the reactor and the habitat protects the habitat itself, inside the crater or operational space of the reactor is a death zone. Astronauts would immediately develop radiation poisoning if entering the area while the reactor is in operation. And since regolith actually reflects neutrons pretty well, many of those neutrons are reflected directly into space, meaning no spacecraft or landers could fly directly over it.

So while we might be able to save thousands of kilograms of launch cost by building our own radiation shields on the Moon, we might also create a no-fly exclusion zone on one particular part of the Moon, just to ensure that astronauts have light and heat during the long, cold lunar nights. That is likely a tradeoff many space enthusiasts will be willing to make. And this study will bring the dream of reliable, continuous nuclear power on our nearest celestial neighbor one step closer to reality.

#6421. Scientists Found a Mushroom That Shouldn’t Exist: It Makes Psychedelics and Deadly Toxins

With this forbidden ‘shroom, the trip to Wonderland is only one way.

Magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms. They have also been used by Indigenous Mesoamerican and South American peoples for centuries to induce visions. Though it was once thought that mushrooms were either magic or poisonous, there is one newly discovered species that, because of a bizarre turn in evolution, produces both psilocybin and lethal amatoxins, possibly as a defense against being eaten. That’s one trip you never want to take.

Galerina indica looks unassuming. Growing on rotting palm trunks in the humid swamps of Florida, this tiny brown mushroom has no fairytale spots or fantastical colors, so it seems like just another fungus bound to be stepped on. Under its dark cap is a darker reality. Matthew Smith of the University of Florida is the state’s official mycologist, identifying species that could be toxic and regularly consulting with Poison Control, and his team was searching for potentially lethal mushrooms when undergrad researcher Andrew Kunik noticed something strange. While documenting fungi, he found that handling G. indica turned it blue. This often occurs in psychedelic mushrooms. Further investigation found that, despite having this telltale characteristic, the mushroom Kunik had been analyzing had a more sinister kind of magic.

“Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, said in a study recently published in Current Biology.

While G. indica did contain psilocybin, it turned out that the ‘shroom also secreted deadly amatoxins. There is no other species of mushroom known for producing both of these substances, and while trippy psiloids have been shown to have possible therapeutic properties, ingesting amatoxins is fatal because these peptides inhibit the enzyme RNA polymerase from creating RNA copies of genes, which leads to organ failure. Fungi are thought to have evolved to produce amatoxins in order to ward off fungivorous creatures such as snails and nematodes. The genes behind production of both psiloids and amatoxins are usually passed down through fungi to their descendants, but the way these genes are acquired is not always so straightforward. Previous studies have suggested they can be horizontally transferred between different fungal species.

Psiloids are known to be synthesized by a cluster of collaborative genes for which evidence of horizontal gene transfer has been found. The same is suspected of amatoxin synthesis, and though there is less evidence for horizontal transfer, it probably began with a fungal donor lineage (which may not have been the same species) that has yet to be identified. Genome analysis has shown that these and other fungal attributes were acquired by genes that were transferred from one species to another growing in the same vicinity. The genus Galerina is already infamous for amatoxins that make many mushrooms within the genus so deadly. How psiloids entered the genus remains a mystery, though just one fateful transfer could have incorporated the genes for amatoxin synthesis into these mushrooms.

What evidence does exist for the transfer of genes that produce psiloids suggests they seeped into a lineage that did not already contain amatoxins, and in a separate evolutionary event, was absorbed by a separate toxic lineage. Kunik’s discovery also revealed how unpredictable fungi can be. The blue pigmentation that is known to be a sign of a magic mushroom comes from psilocin oligomers, molecules linked together from a few repeating structural units, or monomers. Galerina indica has shown that seeing blue does not always mean a mushroom only contains psilocin or psilocybin. While the exact genes that are responsible for amatoxins in this species are still unidentified, and exactly how psiloids evolved in the Galerina genus can only be hypothesized, there is now another thing in Florida more dangerous than alligators.

“G. indica brings together in a single species the biosynthetic systems associated with both ‘magic mushrooms’ and the world’s deadliest poisonous mushrooms,” Kunik and Smith said, “providing a rare natural system for studying how horizontally acquired secondary-metabolite pathways impact organismal fitness.”

#6420. NASA-Funded Study Reveals a Hidden Effect of Space Radiation on the Brain

New NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.

Cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear. A new NASA-funded study in mice found distinct molecular responses to simulated space radiation, raising questions about how prolonged exposure could affect astronauts traveling to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space. These highly energetic particles, often described as cosmic “rays,” can damage spacecraft electronics and potentially affect living tissue. Understanding their effects on the brain is a major concern for future missions beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field.

Researchers at the University of Rochester exposed male and female mice to simulated galactic cosmic radiation at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Led by neuroscience graduate student Mark Osabutey, MBChB, the team used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine nearly 16,000 microglia, the brain’s resident immune cells. This technique allowed scientists to investigate how radiation affected gene activity in individual cells.

The analysis, published in Scientific Reports, identified different molecular responses in males and females. Male microglia showed changes involving cellular stress adaptation and metabolism, while female microglia exhibited broader reductions in immune signaling pathways. Neither group showed widespread inflammatory activation or detectable radiation-related cognitive or behavioral impairment at the time of testing.

“Surprisingly, despite clear molecular changes, we found no widespread inflammatory activation or measurable radiation-associated behavioral impairment at the time we examined,” said Osabutey. The findings suggest that cellular responses to radiation can occur without immediately producing measurable functional problems, although their longer-term effects remain unknown.

Despite these sex-specific differences, researchers identified one response shared by both groups. Levels of FKBP5, a protein involved in regulating cellular stress responses, increased in the cortex and dentate gyrus of male and female mice. These brain regions contribute to functions including cognition, learning, and memory.

“We now need to understand whether FKBP5 plays a protective or harmful role, and how different radiation exposures and other spaceflight stressors influence long-term brain health,” said Osabutey. “Our findings highlight the importance of considering biological sex when assessing neurological risks during spaceflight and identify potential pathways for developing protective strategies.”

University of Rochester Professor of Neuroscience M. Kerry O’Banion, MD, PhD, has investigated the neurological effects of space radiation for more than 15 years. A member of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience, O’Banion previously contributed to research indicating that cosmic radiation could accelerate the onset of Alzheimer’s disease.

“We know cognitive changes from exposure to radiation in space are a real risk,” O’Banion said. “It’s important we understand how brain cells are changed. Knowing which mechanisms are impacted and how may help the development of countermeasures to protect or lessen an astronaut’s exposure to space radiation.”

The latest findings do not establish whether the observed immune cell changes are harmful, protective, or temporary. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether they contribute to neurological problems after prolonged exposure. “Additional studies examining other time points and effects in other experimental systems will be required to understand this further,” O’Banion said.

Osabutey has participated in NASA-funded research since joining O’Banion’s laboratory. In 2023, he received a NASA predoctoral grant augmentation award to investigate changes in microglial populations following exposure to galactic cosmic radiation. He has also presented the laboratory’s research at a NASA conference and attended the European Space Agency Summer School in Darmstadt, Germany.

“Receiving NASA support has allowed me to contribute to research addressing questions of national and international importance,” said Osabutey. “As a physician-scientist in training, I could not have asked for a better environment in which to train, and the experience has taught me how to pursue meaningful scientific questions through rigorous basic/translational investigation and collaboration, skills that I will carry forward in my future efforts to better understand brain injury and neurological disease.”

The research involved a broader collaboration between University of Rochester scientists and personnel at Brookhaven National Laboratory, where particle accelerators generate radiation conditions relevant to spaceflight.

“Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows have been an essential part of our NASA research effort,” O’Banion said. “It’s comprised of a large team that includes the outstanding organizational skills of our long-time senior research technician, Lee Trojanczyk, as well as support personnel at Brookhaven National Labs. Over time, nearly a dozen University of Rochester trainees have contributed to this work.”

Reference: “Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals sex-specific microglial responses to simulated galactic cosmic radiation without broad inflammatory activation” by Mark A. Osabutey, Lia Calcines-Rodríguez, Lee A. Trojanczyk, John A. Olschowka and M. Kerry O’Banion, 20 November 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-77661-9

This research was supported by a NASA grant and a NASA Human Research Program Grant Augmentation Award.

#6419. ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula. Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled "The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530â0213." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530â0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ringâfirst evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon starâand a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

âMost of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a starâs death throes,â said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. âItâs the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.â

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530âs central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

âDying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,â said Sahai. âIRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation weâve been using.â

IRAS 06530 also has a chemical composition that's challenging to understand. It's significantly enriched in 13C, 17O, and modestly enriched in 15N.

"Compared with solar values, the torus of IRAS 06530 appears to be significantly (modestly) enriched in 13C and 17O (15N), as wellâa pattern of rare-isotope enrichment inconsistent with standard nucleosynthesis models," the authors write.

Â¹Â³C and Â¹â·O are expected, but Â¹âµN isn't. It should be destroyed and depleted to solar levels. Again, a binary companion could be one explanation for this anomaly, and future observations might find one. It's also possible that atypical bursts of nuclear burning are responsible, but that's beyond the scope of this work.

Finding the first direct evidence of a dying star's thermal pulse, something indicated by theory, is the kind of progress astrophysicists hope to make.

âItâs essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, weâve mostly inferred from theoretical models,â said Sahai. âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6417. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability

#6416. This Guy Found a Security Camera’s Exact Location Using Only the Sound of Two Planes

Add the Doppler effect to the growing list of things that can be used as surveillance tools.

Geoguessr is a widely popular online geography game where players glimpse one still frame from Google Street View and then attempt to pinpoint the exact location on a world map. Many things can be helpful hints—the design of road signs, the format of license plates, specific road markings as well as surrounding trees and landscapes. However, a YouTuber named colsto took this idea to a whole new level by geolocating an incredibly grainy video by just its captured audio.

Mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints. No one nearby is talking about this “da Bears” game with a thick Chicago accent, for example. But buried within the security camera’s spectrogram (visual display of frequencies over time) is a clue—two of them, in fact. To the uninitiated they look relatively innocuous two sloping lights roughly 920 seconds apart, but colsto recognized these lines as the Doppler effect signatures of a two planes passing overhead.

To start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude. Websites like Flightradar24 rely on this data to provide a real-time snapshot of on-going flights around the world. Colsto first cross-referenced this data and winnowed potential candidates by choosing parameters featuring two planes the right speed and the right distance away while still traveling within 920 seconds of each other. The results weren’t promising.

“That gave us…roughly 70,000 points,” colsto says in the video. “Now, adding on to all that logic, the silence filter—where that point doesn’t hear another flight between the two events—drops from 70,000 to 15,000. Even with all those constraints, there is just so much land area and so many flights that 15,000 points still meet all those criteria.”

Instead of going through each data point, ruling out why it doesn’t fit and refining the search parameters, colsto returned to the Doppler curves and revised one of the search’s original assumptions. These two curves didn’t represent a perfect Doppler curve because planes are constantly adjusting speed and heading, and that information—no matter how slight—is locked away within these two curves. So colsto modeled the Doppler curves to create a flight path that could then be checked against 15,000 possible points.

“The Doppler curve is a function of the radial velocity of the plane with respect to the observer,” colsto says in the video. “The Doppler curve would change depending on the plane geometry.”

Eventually, colsto found the exact security camera located in Oyster Bay in Long Island, New York, that captured the grainy security footage of the pixelated tree line.

“I’m trying to fear monger with this video. The odds that someone can and does actually do this is pretty slim,” colsto said at the video’s conclusion. “In reality, there’s probably one hundred easier ways to find you than this.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6415. Scientists Discover a Potential New Way To Treat Diabetes – No Insulin Required

A discovery in animal muscle suggests that the body’s natural ability to absorb sugar without insulin could be harnessed to develop new diabetes treatments.

For people with diabetes or insulin resistance, controlling blood sugar can be difficult because their muscles do not respond effectively to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Muscles, however, have another way of absorbing glucose that does not require insulin. Understanding how this process works could give researchers an entirely new way to treat high blood sugar.

Scientists at the University of Cincinnati (UC) College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown pathway that allows skeletal muscles to absorb glucose independently of insulin. Their findings, published in the Nature Portfolio journal Communications Biology, could provide a new target for treating diabetes, hyperglycemia, and insulin resistance.

Skeletal muscle makes up about 40% of the human body and plays a major role in regulating blood sugar. After a meal, rising insulin levels stimulate muscles to absorb and store up to 90% of ingested glucose through a transport protein called GLUT4, which helps glucose enter muscle cells.

During exercise or stress, insulin levels drop, yet working muscles can absorb glucose at rates up to 100 times higher than after a meal to meet the energy demands of contraction. How muscles manage this without insulin has remained a mystery despite decades of research.

To investigate, the researchers developed a way to measure glucose uptake independently of insulin. They used glucose derivatives that could be carried by a family of transport proteins known as SGLTs but not by GLUT4. The team tested these derivatives in isolated muscles from animal models, using electrical stimulation to reproduce the contractions of working muscles.

“We showed that if we stimulate muscle to contract in insulin-free conditions, it can take up a lot of glucose from a pathway that’s not GLUT4,” said Judith A. Heiny, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and professor emerita in the Division of Neurobiology and Integrative Physiology in UC’s Department of Biomedical Sciences, whose laboratory led the research.

The researchers named the newly identified pathway mSGLT. It shares properties with SGLT2, a glucose transporter in the kidneys that is already targeted by widely used diabetes medications such as Jardiance. These drugs lower blood sugar by increasing the amount of glucose expelled through urine. Targeting a similar transport mechanism in muscles could offer another way to remove excess glucose from the bloodstream.

“This insulin-independent process uses a glucose transport protein in skeletal muscle and may offer a drug target for controlling blood sugar,” said Heiny. “The skeletal musculature is the natural depot for glucose. It has a huge capacity to regulate blood sugar, which can be a struggle for those with diabetes and insulin resistance.”

“A therapy that targets glucose uptake by skeletal muscles could be as impactful as SGLT2 inhibitors that lower blood sugar by stimulating the kidneys to excrete excess glucose in the urine,” said Natalie Norman, PhD, the study’s first author. Norman contributed to the research as a UC graduate student and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

Working with collaborators at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the team also developed a new technique for measuring glucose uptake using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), an analytical technique that could have applications beyond diabetes research.

“I expect our method will be ideal for studying biological processes that require simultaneous tracking of multiple molecules,” said Julio Landero, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and associate professor and director of a trace metals lab at Mount Sinai.

Although the researchers have established how the pathway behaves in isolated animal muscles, they have yet to identify the specific transport protein responsible or determine whether targeting it can improve blood sugar regulation.

“This study defines the core properties of mSGLT in muscle. Studies are underway to identify the gene and protein at the molecular level,” said Heiny.

Reference: “Insulin-independent glucose uptake into mouse skeletal muscle by a sodium/glucose linked transporter” by Natalie J. Norman, Tatiana L. Radzyukevich, Peter W. Chomczynski, Michal Rymaszewski, Izabela D. Fokt, Waldemar Priebe, Lucas Schmidt, Tiffany Zhu, Bryan Mackenzie, Julio A. Landero and Judith A. Heiny, 19 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-10848-y

The National Institutes of Health, the UC College of Medicine and private philanthropy funded this research.

#6414. The Event Horizon Telescope Views the Dynamics and Geometry of a Black Hole Jet in Extreme Detail

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jet emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at sub-parsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers - Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) - that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, the jet coming from its center is powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

An image of the core region of Messier 87, a supermassive black hole, processed from an array of radio telescopes known as the EHT with colours indicating brightness temperature (Credit: Event Horizon Telescope)

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik MÃ¼ller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut fÃ¼r Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alpes to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain. They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine, and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019. As MÃ¼ller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software were used during early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

Illustration of the multiwavelength 3C 279 jet structure in April 2017. The observing epochs, arrays, and wavelengths are noted in each panel. Credit: J.Y. Kim/MPIfR/VLBA and GMVA/EHT

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented towards our instruments, MÃ¼ller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending towards Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said MÃ¼ller:

We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.

While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen. Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images on how it behaves at the sub-parsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said MÃ¼ller:

This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.

We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.

Further Reading: Astronomy & Astrophysics
